title: London's Beloved Dishoom Secures Its Manhattan Address — and It's Bringing Friends
excerpt: The LVMH-backed Bombay café chain has locked in a NoMad location for its U.S. debut, joining a wave of British Indian restaurants crossing the Atlantic.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Dishoom's first U.S. restaurant will open in Manhattan's NoMad neighborhood in 2027.
  • A previous pop-up in 2024 sold out 6,000 reservations in four minutes, with a 20,000 waitlist.
  • Dishoom received a $400 million investment from L Catterton, enabling its international expansion.
  • Over 4.4 million people in the U.S. identify as part of the Indian diaspora, influencing cuisine trends.
  • Dishoom plans to open 2-3 U.S. locations annually, with potential expansions to Boston and Chicago.
Dishoom's Journey to New York

The wait is nearly over. Dishoom, the London-born Indian restaurant chain that has inspired cultlike devotion for its retro Bombay café atmosphere and irresistible comfort food, has secured a site for its first-ever American restaurant — and it is landing in one of Manhattan's most coveted dining neighborhoods. The restaurant will open at 11 East 26th Street in NoMad, the corridor north of Madison Square Park that has become ground zero for high-profile restaurant openings in New York. A debut is targeted for 2027, according to recent reports, making it the culmination of a transatlantic courtship that has lasted the better part of a decade. ## From Pop-Up Frenzy to Permanent Address Dishoom's road to New York has been anything but quiet. In August 2024, the group staged a two-week breakfast pop-up at Pastis, the legendary French brasserie in the Meatpacking District. The result was pandemonium: 6,000 reservation slots sold out in four and a half minutes. A waitlist of 20,000 followed. The pop-up confirmed what co-founder Kavi Thakrar had suspected since at least 2016: New York was ready for Dishoom. But it took time — and money — to get the pieces in place. Last summer, Dishoom received its first-ever outside investment: a deal with L Catterton, the private equity firm that is 40% owned by LVMH, the luxury conglomerate behind Louis Vuitton and Moët Hennessy. The investment reportedly valued Dishoom at approximately $400 million, giving the group the financial firepower for international expansion while preserving the family's operational control. ## The Dishoom Effect Founded in 2010 by cousins Shamil and Kavi Thakrar, Dishoom channels the spirit of Bombay's vanishing Irani cafés — establishments opened by Zoroastrian immigrants from Iran in the early 20th century that became democratic gathering places for artists, writers, students, and workers. The restaurants are immersive: vintage photographs, ceiling fans, distressed wood, and an atmosphere that makes you feel like you have stumbled into a time capsule. But the food is the real draw. Dishoom's black dal — simmered for 24 hours — has achieved near-mythical status. The bacon naan roll, a cheekily Anglo-Indian invention, moves in staggering volumes. Gunpowder potatoes, chicken ruby curry, and chile cheese toast round out a menu that is both deeply traditional and effortlessly modern. Today, the group operates more than 15 restaurants across the U.K. (including the Dishoom and Permit Room brands), serves over 100,000 diners a week, and employs around 2,000 people. The Leeds location — their latest — opened to enormous demand earlier this month. ## Not Coming Alone What makes Dishoom's arrival especially significant is that it is not an isolated event. A full wave of acclaimed British Indian restaurants is crossing the Atlantic simultaneously: **Ambassadors Clubhouse**, the Punjabi concept from JKS Restaurants — the same group behind Gymkhana — has signed a ground-floor lease at the A24 building (yes, the film company) at 1245 Broadway in NoMad, with a fall opening planned. **Darjeeling Express**, Asma Khan's celebrated restaurant (and Netflix "Chef's Table" subject), is working toward a Manhattan opening following a sold-out pop-up.

**Kricket**, the Indian small plates concept, is also reportedly eyeing a 2027 Manhattan launch. And Gymkhana itself already made its U.S. debut at the Aria Resort & Casino in Las Vegas, bringing two Michelin stars to the Strip for the first time. ## Why Now? Several forces have converged. The Indian diaspora in America has reached a critical mass — over 4.4 million, with outsized economic influence in cities like New York, San Francisco, and Chicago. A generation of Indian-American chefs (Chintan Pandya at Dhamaka, Vijay Kumar at Semma) has already proven that ambitious Indian food can thrive in New York beyond the old curry-house model. "There are so many young professionals, second-generation, third-generation people running businesses," Thakrar told the New York Times. "Indian food is finally part of the city's fabric." But the British Indian angle adds a layer of nuance. Indian cuisine in Britain has had over 70 years to evolve, experiment, and refine itself — from the first curry houses of Brick Lane to the molecular gastronomy of Gaggan Anand. The restaurants crossing the Atlantic now carry that accumulated wisdom: they know how to present Indian food to a Western audience without diluting it. ## What's Next

Dishoom plans to open two to three sites per year in the U.S., with CEO Brian Trollip noting that teams have also explored sites in Boston, Chicago, and Washington, D.C. There is even talk of a Dishoom hotel, inspired by the overnight suites above its Permit Room bar in London's Notting Hill, where guests are woken with hot chai and a bacon naan. For now, the NoMad address is the focus — and the New York Indian food scene is about to get a lot more interesting. The question is no longer whether Indian cuisine can be mainstream in America. It is whether anyone will be able to get a reservation.
